clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant deficiency of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, the penultimate enzyme of haem biosynthesis, notably prevalent in the Afrikaner population owing to a founder mutation
A mixed porphyria that can cause both acute neurovisceral attacks (as in acute intermittent porphyria) and chronic photocutaneous skin fragility
Skin lesions comprise blistering, erosions, milia and fragility on sun-exposed areas, clinically indistinguishable from porphyria cutanea tarda
During acute attacks urinary ALA and PBG rise, but the discriminating feature is a characteristic plasma fluorescence emission peak around the high 620s nanometre range
Faecal porphyrin analysis typically shows raised protoporphyrin and coproporphyrin, helping distinguish it from other acute porphyrias
Acute attacks share the same drug, fasting and hormonal triggers as acute intermittent porphyria and are managed similarly with trigger removal, glucose loading and intravenous haem
Cutaneous disease is managed largely by sun protection and avoidance of skin trauma rather than by the measures effective in porphyria cutanea tarda
reference.pathophysiology: Variegate porphyria arises from reduced activity of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, the seventh enzyme of the haem pathway, which oxidises protoporphyrinogen to protoporphyrin. Deficiency causes accumulation of protoporphyrinogen and back-up of upstream intermediates. The photoreactive porphyrins deposited in the skin generate reactive oxygen species on light exposure, causing the blistering photodermatosis, while induction of hepatic ALA synthase during metabolic stress raises the neurotoxic precursors ALA and PBG that drive acute neurovisceral attacks. The dual accumulation explains the mixed acute and cutaneous phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Porphyria cutanea tarda (identical skin picture but no acute attacks)
Hereditary coproporphyria (the other mixed acute porphyria)
Acute intermittent porphyria during a neurovisceral attack
Pseudoporphyria from drugs or renal dialysis
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and other subepidermal blistering disorders
Surgical acute abdomen during an attack
additionalInvestigations: Plasma fluorescence scanning showing the characteristic emission peak diagnostic of variegate porphyria
Urinary ALA and PBG during symptomatic attacks
Molecular genetic testing of the PPOX gene for confirmation and family screening
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to confirm subepidermal bullae and exclude mimics
Serum sodium and renal function during acute attacks
redFlags: Progressive motor neuropathy or respiratory compromise during an acute attack
Seizures with hyponatraemia during an attack
Severe photocutaneous ulceration with secondary infection
Exposure to a known porphyrinogenic drug in a symptomatic patient
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous manifestations tend to persist while acute attacks are usually preventable with trigger avoidance; most patients maintain a good quality of life, though severe attacks carry the same neurological risks as other acute porphyrias.
pitfalls: Mistaking the skin disease for porphyria cutanea tarda and applying inappropriate therapy
Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs that precipitate acute attacks
Relying on urinary studies alone and missing the diagnosis between attacks when they may be near normal
Failing to protect skin from sunlight and trauma
Not screening at-risk relatives, particularly in founder populations
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Prevent acute attacks by avoiding porphyrinogenic drugs, alcohol and fasting, and by promptly treating intercurrent infection and other metabolic stressors
Treat acute neurovisceral attacks with intravenous haem arginate and carbohydrate glucose loading, alongside porphyria-safe analgesia, antiemetics and management of autonomic features
Correct attack-related hyponatraemia and treat seizures with porphyria-safe anticonvulsants
Manage the photocutaneous disease with sun avoidance, protective clothing and barrier photoprotection, with careful skin care to limit fragility, blistering and erosions
Provide the patient with a list of safe and unsafe drugs and clear guidance to seek urgent care during attacks
Undertake long-term surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma and chronic kidney disease
Manage through a specialist porphyria centre and offer genetic counselling with family screening for the PPOX variant
